outcome: Since 26 January 2024 neither the Kelvin problem nor the optimality of the Weaire–Phelan structure has been settled. The window holds only restricted results: two preprints of 1 and 2 September 2026 (Hales and Song, arXiv:2609.00997; Cesaroni and Novaga, arXiv:2609.02384) that prove Bezdek's truncated-octahedron conjecture for parallelohedra, i.e. equal-volume partitions into translative convex tiles, which both papers say does not solve the Kelvin problem; a later local-stability preprint by Song (arXiv:2609.03093); and earlier lattice and perimeter-minimisation papers that restate the problem as open. The Hales–Song paper credits GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT with a substantial role in the proof.
problem_asks: Read from the frozen statement, the bullet asks for two things. (1) The Kelvin problem: among all partitions of Euclidean space into cells of equal volume (the frozen wording names no dimension; the classical case is R^3), find the partition that minimises total interfacial surface area, i.e. identify the minimiser and its shape. (2) The optimality of the Weaire–Phelan structure as a solution of (1): show that the Weaire–Phelan structure, a periodic partition with two cell types and curved faces, has least surface area among all equal-volume partitions. The bullet's own title names both parts, and they are separate questions: a proof that Weaire–Phelan beats Kelvin's foam would answer neither. The bullet does not say periodic, lattice, polyhedral or translative; those are restrictions that the literature studies, and they are not the bullet unless the judging pass decides otherwise. Reading flagged for the judging pass: I take 'partitions of space' as all equal-volume partitions, not only periodic ones.

events.what_happened: Denis Weaire and Robert Phelan found, by numerical minimisation in the Surface Evolver program, a periodic partition of space into equal-volume cells (a unit cell of eight cells of two types: six 14-faced and two 12-faced, with curved faces) whose total interface area is about 0.3% below that of Kelvin's truncated-octahedron foam. The paper is 'A counter-example to Kelvin's conjecture on minimal surfaces', Philosophical Magazine Letters 69(2), 1994; Wikipedia and Brakke date the discovery to 1993. Wikipedia's article (opened) says 'Although numerical experiments suggest that the Weaire–Phelan structure is optimal, this remains unproven.' The paper itself was not opened.
events.revisions: Discovery reported as 1993 (Wikipedia; Brakke); publication 1994 (Wikipedia, Phil. Mag. Lett. 69(2)). The 1994 publication year is used as the first written argument, since no earlier written version was found.
events.delivers: Disproves Kelvin's conjecture that Kelvin's truncated-octahedron foam has least area: it exhibits a periodic equal-volume partition with about 0.3% less area. Numerical evidence only at this stage. Establishes nothing about whether the Weaire–Phelan structure is minimal.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the minimiser of the Kelvin problem is not identified, and the optimality of Weaire–Phelan is unproven.

checked_by.who: R. Kusner and J. Sullivan (analytic comparison; see event kusner-sullivan-1996)
checked_by.qualification: Geometers working on minimal surfaces and foams
checked_by.what_they_did: Proved analytically that the polyhedral Weaire–Phelan foam has less area than any foam with Kelvin's topology. This checks the numerical comparison only within that topology class, not optimality.
checked_by.where: https://kenbrakke.com/kelvin/kelvin.html (secondary report; Kusner–Sullivan paper not opened)

events.directly_checkable: The periodic cell can be checked by computing its surface area and cell volumes in Surface Evolver; Brakke's page refers to datafiles for both partitions. Not run.
events.doubts: The original evidence is numerical (Surface Evolver). Kusner and Sullivan removed the numerical doubt for the comparison within Kelvin's topology. Brakke's page says 'There is no proof that the Weaire–Phelan partition is optimal'. Not a doubt about the disproof, but the limit of what it shows.
events.direction: Cuts against the claim that Kelvin's foam is the minimiser of the equal-volume problem. Says nothing decisive about whether Weaire–Phelan is the minimiser.
events.object: A periodic partition of R^3 into equal-volume cells: the Weaire–Phelan foam, a unit cell of eight cells of two types (six 14-faced and two 12-faced, with irregular faces, some curved), found numerically with Surface Evolver. Its total area is about 0.3% below Kelvin's bitruncated-honeycomb foam (isoperimetric quotient 0.764, per Brakke and the Opsomer–Vandewalle paper). It is an explicit numerical construction, not an existence proof.

events.what_happened: R. Kusner and J. Sullivan proved analytically that the polyhedral Weaire–Phelan foam has less total area than any foam sharing Kelvin's combinatorial topology. Brakke's page (opened) reports the result, which it describes as removing doubts about numerical error. The source is cited as 'Comparing the Weaire–Phelan equal-volume foam to Kelvin's foam', Forma (1996), taken from a bibliographic reference seen in search; the paper itself was not opened.
events.revisions: None found. Forma publication year is from a reference-list entry, not verified.
events.delivers: Within the class of foams with Kelvin's topology, the polyhedral Weaire–Phelan foam beats Kelvin's foam analytically. Restricted to that topology class, and it does not show Weaire–Phelan is minimal among all equal-volume partitions.
events.remains: Optimality of Weaire–Phelan among all equal-volume partitions; the minimiser of the Kelvin problem over all partitions. Brakke: 'There is no proof that the Weaire–Phelan partition is optimal.'

checked_by.who: Ken Brakke (Susquehanna University; developer of Surface Evolver)
checked_by.qualification: Developer of the numerical tool used for the original comparison
checked_by.what_they_did: Reports the Kusner–Sullivan analytic proof on his Kelvin page; no independent check described

events.doubts: Limited to the Kelvin topology, as Brakke states. The Forma paper was not read, so the details of the proof are not checked here.
events.direction: Supports Weaire–Phelan over Kelvin's foam within the Kelvin topology class. Does not bear on whether Weaire–Phelan is minimal.

events.what_happened: T. C. Hales, 'The Honeycomb Conjecture' (arXiv:math/9906042, submitted 8 June 1999; Discrete & Computational Geometry 25 (2001) 1–22). Any partition of the plane into regions of equal area has average perimeter at least that of the regular hexagonal tiling. This is the two-dimensional analogue of the Kelvin problem. Seen in search snippets and a Wikipedia search result; the arXiv abstract and the journal DOI were not opened.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 8 Jun 1999; v2 20 May 2002; journal version DCG 2001.
events.delivers: Settles the planar analogue (dimension 2, equal areas, perimeter). Does not touch the three-dimensional problem.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks, which is three-dimensional (or unspecified-dimension) space.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the published version
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the honeycomb paper, 25(1), 2001, pp. 1–22 (per search snippet; not opened)

events.direction: Confirms the honeycomb (hexagonal) answer in two dimensions. Analogue only; no direction on the three-dimensional problem.

events.what_happened: Ruggero Gabbrielli (then at the University of Bath) proposed a periodic foam built from modified Voronoi diagrams of point sets generated by the Swift–Hohenberg equation, with four cell types and quadrilateral, pentagonal and hexagonal faces. Press coverage (ScienceDaily, Sept 2009) and search snippets say it has less area than Kelvin's foam but more than Weaire–Phelan. Neither the paper nor the press release was opened.
events.revisions: None found. Venue and month not confirmed.
events.delivers: A new periodic partition with area below Kelvin's foam and above Weaire–Phelan. It does not beat Weaire–Phelan. Whether its cells have equal volume was not verified.
events.doubts: Only search snippets were read; the equal-volume condition and the area values were not checked against the paper.
events.direction: Cuts against Kelvin's foam as minimiser, but not against Weaire–Phelan, by its own account.
events.object: A periodic partition with four cell types and quadrilateral, pentagonal and hexagonal faces, with area between the Kelvin and Weaire–Phelan values (per search snippets; not verified).

events.what_happened: Jin-ichi Itoh and Chie Nara, Kumamoto Journal of Mathematics 23 (2010). Per a search snippet, the truncated octahedron minimises surface area among polyhedral unfoldings of a doubly covered cuboid with edge ratio √2:√2:1, a restricted 'orthic' version of Kelvin's conjecture. The PDF was fetched but returned as binary that I could not read, so this is from search snippets only.
events.delivers: Restricted to polyhedral unfoldings of one doubly covered cuboid. Not the Kelvin problem.
events.direction: Supports the truncated octahedron in a restricted class; no counterexample.

events.what_happened: E. Opsomer and N. Vandewalle, 'Novel structures for optimal space partitions', New Journal of Physics 18 (2016) 103008, published 7 Oct 2016. A stochastic search maximising the mean isoperimeter Q, not total area, found structures including N=24 (cells with 12 and 16 faces), N=40 and A15* (N=8). Their cell volumes are unequal, and they have uncurved facets. Equal-volume cases include N=9 with a higher isoperimeter than Kelvin's; the paper states the Weaire–Phelan structure keeps the highest known Q′ for equal-volume polyhedra. The paper says its method 'is not relevant for total area minimization'. Opened.
events.revisions: No earlier preprint found; the journal publication date is used because no earlier written version was found.
events.delivers: Partitions with higher isoperimeter Q than Weaire–Phelan, but with unequal cell volumes (N=24, N=40), so outside the equal-volume Kelvin problem. Total area is not compared, and the paper disclaims total-area minimisation.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks, for the equal-volume total-area problem.

checked_by.who: New Journal of Physics (peer-reviewed journal; IOP Publishing)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the published version

events.directly_checkable: Cell structures are given in the paper's tables; not checked.
events.doubts: The optimised quantity is the isoperimeter Q, not total area, and the equal-volume requirement is violated for the structures that beat Weaire–Phelan.
events.direction: Cuts against Weaire–Phelan only on the isoperimeter Q with unequal volumes, which is not the bullet's quantity. Does not cut against Weaire–Phelan for equal-volume total area.
events.object: A 24-cell polyhedral partition (cells with 12 and 16 faces; volume fluctuation 0.10063; uncurved facets) with isoperimeter Q′ = 0.76504, reported to exceed Weaire–Phelan's Q′ = 0.764. Found numerically by stochastic optimisation, not by a construction or existence proof. Its cells do not have equal volume.

events.what_happened: Zsolt Lángi, 'An isoperimetric problem for three-dimensional parallelohedra' (arXiv:2102.11621, Feb 2021; Pacific Journal of Mathematics 316 (2022) 169–181). Among parallelohedra of unit volume, the regular truncated octahedron has least mean width. This is a different functional from surface area. Seen in search snippets; neither the arXiv abstract nor the PJM page was opened.
events.delivers: Mean width, not surface area, among parallelohedra. A different functional, so not a result on the bullet's quantity.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for the published version

events.direction: Consistent with the truncated octahedron being extremal among parallelohedra for mean width. Not a surface-area result.

events.what_happened: A. Cesaroni and M. Novaga, 'Minimal periodic foams with equal cells' (arXiv:2302.07112, 14 Feb 2023; v2 12 Jul 2023). Abstract: 'We show existence of periodic foams with equal cells in R^n minimizing an anisotropic perimeter.' The abstract page does not mention the Kelvin problem or Weaire–Phelan. Opened (abstract page only).
events.delivers: Existence of minimisers for an anisotropic perimeter among periodic equal-cell foams. Does not identify the minimiser and uses a different functional.
events.doubts: Only the abstract page was read.
events.direction: No direction on the Kelvin problem as stated.

events.what_happened: A. Cesaroni and M. Novaga, 'Minimal periodic foams with fixed inradius' (arXiv:2407.07534; v1 10 Jul 2024, v3 16 Jul 2024). Shows existence and regularity of periodic tilings of Euclidean space into equal cells, each containing a ball of fixed radius, minimising the classical or fractional perimeter, with qualitative properties in dimensions 3 and 4. Its introduction states that 'The Kelvin problem remains open for every N≥3, even if one restricts to lattice tilings', that the Weaire–Phelan counterexample does not apply to lattice tilings, and that for the parallelohedral restriction in dimension 3 'The identification of the shape of the solution is still open.' Opened (abstract page and HTML v3). A journal listing (Mathematika, 2025) appeared in search, not verified.
events.revisions: v1 10 Jul 2024; v2 11 Jul 2024; v3 16 Jul 2024. Journal publication per search only (Mathematika 2025), not verified.
events.delivers: Existence and regularity of minimisers for fixed-inradius equal-cell periodic tilings with a classical or fractional perimeter. Does not identify any minimiser, and does not establish any restricted case of the equal-volume problem.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. Its own text says the lattice-periodic problem, and the parallelohedral restriction in dimension 3, have unidentified minimisers.
events.doubts: Its own status claim is that the problem is open. Its later journal publication, if it happened, was not verified.
events.direction: No counterexample. Its status claim is that the Kelvin problem and its lattice and parallelohedral restrictions are open as of July 2024, which is the baseline for the September 2026 restricted results.

events.what_happened: F. Nobili and M. Novaga, 'Lattice tilings with minimal perimeter and unequal volumes' (arXiv:2406.12461, submitted 18 Jun 2024). Studies periodic tessellations with unequal cells and minimising perimeter; in the plane, hexagonal tilings are optimal among partitions with almost equal areas. The introduction restates Kelvin's problem and says 'so that the original problem remains open, and the same holds in higher dimensions.' Opened (abstract page and HTML v1).
events.revisions: v1 only, per the abstract page.
events.delivers: Results for unequal-volume tilings. Nothing on equal-volume partitions in three dimensions.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. Its introduction records the original problem as open.
events.direction: No direction on the equal-volume problem. Records the problem as open as of June 2024.

events.what_happened: A. Cesaroni and M. Novaga, 'Local minimality of the truncated octahedron for the isoperimetric problem on parallelohedra' (arXiv:2603.27221, submitted 28 Mar 2026; math.MG, math.CO). For three-dimensional lattice Voronoi cells, a closed formula for the scale-invariant isoperimetric quotient F; BCC is a strict local minimiser at fixed volume, FCC and SC are not local minimisers, and BCC is the global minimiser in a family interpolating BCC and FCC. The introduction frames the work through the Kelvin problem and the Weaire–Phelan counterexample. The abstract page does not mention Kelvin; the HTML introduction does. Opened (abstract page and HTML v1). The Bollettino UMI publication (2026) appears only in a later preprint's reference list; not verified.
events.revisions: v1 only per the abstract page. Journal: Boll. Unione Mat. Ital. (2026), per a reference in arXiv:2609.02384 (unverified).
events.delivers: Local minimality of the BCC lattice's Voronoi cell (truncated octahedron) for F among lattice Voronoi cells, plus minimality within one lattice family. Restricted to lattice Voronoi cells (periodic lattice tilings with equal cells).
events.remains: The Kelvin problem over all partitions; global minimality among lattices; the parallelohedral case beyond local (addressed in the September 2026 events); Weaire–Phelan optimality.
events.directly_checkable: The BCC lattice's Voronoi cell is the truncated octahedron; the closed formula for F is in the paper. Not checked.
events.doubts: No public reading of the argument found. The journal status is not verified.
events.direction: Consistent with the truncated octahedron (Kelvin's cell) being locally optimal among lattice Voronoi cells. Restricted to lattices; no bearing on Weaire–Phelan, whose cells are not a lattice Voronoi tiling.

events.what_happened: Thomas Hales and Lark Song, 'The Truncated Octahedral Conjecture' (arXiv:2609.00997, v1 submitted 1 Sep 2026, 45 pp.; v2 11 Sep 2026, shortened to about 23 pp.). Claims that, among three-dimensional parallelohedra of fixed volume, the Archimedean truncated octahedron uniquely minimises surface area. This is Bezdek's 2006 conjecture; Theorem 1.1 (as printed in v1) bounds the isoperimetric quotient below by 3(1+2√3)/4^(2/3), with equality only for truncated octahedra. Corollary for lattice Voronoi cells. One scalar inequality is verified by an exact computer-assisted Bernstein certificate, with an appendix and accompanying program. The introduction says: 'Bezdek's conjecture can be interpreted as a modification of the original Kelvin problem that restricts the equal-volume partitions of space to tilings by parallelohedra.' Also a 10 Sep 2026 Pittsburgh seminar listing with the abstract 'This research is joint work with Lark Song, in partnership with AI.' Opened (arXiv abs v1; HTML v1 and v2 via a summarising fetch).
events.revisions: v1 1 Sep 2026 (45 pp.); v2 11 Sep 2026 (about 23 pp.; per tracker, 'simplifies the proof by introducing the Bernstein certificate sooner'). The AI-use statement appears in a 'Statement on AI use' section in v1 and in an 'AI interactions' part of the acknowledgements in v2 (per summarising fetches).
events.delivers: For parallelohedra (convex polyhedra that tile space by translations of one cell) of fixed volume, the regular truncated octahedron uniquely minimises the isoperimetric quotient, with a corollary for lattice Voronoi cells. Restricted to translative tilings by one convex cell. Outside the class: curved faces, non-congruent cells, and non-translational periodic partitions. Claimed, not refereed.
events.remains: The Kelvin problem over all equal-volume partitions (curved faces, non-congruent cells, non-translational periodic partitions). The optimality of Weaire–Phelan. Weaire–Phelan has two cell types and is not a translative tiling by one cell, so on my reading it lies outside this class; the authors do not discuss Weaire–Phelan.

checked_by.who: kingy.ai Breakthrough Tracker (third-party aggregator; not a reading of the argument)
checked_by.qualification: Not a mathematical reviewer. The record was added 4 Sep 2026 and checked 2 Oct 2026.
checked_by.what_they_did: Labelled the result 'Provisional · Provisional computer-assisted proof'. Says this maintenance cycle did not independently replay the full computation and that no independent replay was located. Records that the manuscript is not peer reviewed.

events.directly_checkable: The exact scalar certificate (appendix, 'A.6 Exact certificate criterion') and the accompanying program, which the authors say 'reconstructs every polynomial and every Bernstein coefficient from the displayed formulas; no floating-point estimate enters the proof'. Neither was replayed here. No Lean or Coq formalisation was found.
events.doubts: (a) Unrefereed first-version preprint; v2 is a substantially shortened revision. (b) One scalar inequality rests on computer-assisted exact certificates that the tracker says were not independently replayed. (c) The authors credit an AI model with a substantial role in the proof (see ai). (d) No public reading of the argument by a mathematician was found. (e) Later papers cite it as a complete resolution of the restricted conjecture (see later_work_cites_it), which describes the claim, not an outside verification. No specific error identified in any source.
events.direction: Cuts for Bezdek's conjecture: the truncated octahedron is claimed to minimise surface area among parallelohedra of fixed volume. Against the bullet's question, this is a restricted class: it neither identifies the minimiser of the general Kelvin problem nor bears on Weaire–Phelan's optimality.

systems.name: GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors' 'Statement on AI use' in v1: the model was used in a substantial way at all stages of the project. Per the v2 acknowledgements (summarising fetch, not verbatim), it was used for proof discovery, code, and drafting. The authors say 'ChatGPT also provided editorial suggestions and feedback on the manuscript' and that they 'take full responsibility for the proof, the computer code, and the supplied certificate'. Whether the model's contribution is load-bearing is for the judging pass; the authors' own words are 'proof discovery' (v2, via summary) and 'used in a substantial way at all stages' (v1).
systems.basis_quote: A large language model (GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT) was used in a substantial way at all stages of this project.

events.what_happened: A. Cesaroni and M. Novaga, 'The truncated octahedron minimizes surface area among parallelohedra of equal volume' (arXiv:2609.02384, v1 2 Sep 2026; v2 9 Sep 2026). Claims the same statement as Hales–Song: the regular truncated octahedron uniquely minimises the isoperimetric quotient among three-dimensional parallelohedra of fixed volume, with bound 3(1+2√3)/4^(2/3). For the non-truncated Fedorov types, a stronger sharp bound, attained uniquely by the regular rhombic dodecahedron. The introduction says 'Theorem 1.1 does not address arbitrary periodic equal-volume partitions, and hence does not solve the Kelvin problem', and that 'After this work was completed, we became aware of an independent proof of the Truncated Octahedron Conjecture by Thomas Hales and Lark Song.' Opened (abstract page, v1 and v2 pages, and HTML v1 first 100,000 characters; the remainder was not read).
events.revisions: v1 2 Sep 2026; v2 9 Sep 2026 (per the arXiv comments: 'corrected some misprints, and moreover reorganized some parts (in particular relative to the entropy contraction estimates)').
events.delivers: The same restricted class as Hales–Song: parallelohedra of fixed volume, with the truncated octahedron as unique minimiser, and a stronger bound for non-truncated Fedorov types. Explicitly not arbitrary periodic equal-volume partitions, per the authors.
events.remains: The Kelvin problem over all equal-volume partitions; the optimality of Weaire–Phelan. The authors say the result 'does not solve the Kelvin problem'.
events.doubts: No public reading of the argument by a mathematician was found. Its agreement with Hales–Song is agreement on the conclusion; the authors say they became aware of Hales–Song after their own work was complete, and it is not a check of the Hales–Song certificate. No specific error identified.
events.direction: Same as Hales–Song: cuts for Bezdek's restricted conjecture. Not a bearing on the Kelvin problem as stated, by the authors' own account.

systems.name: ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Sol)
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors: used during the preparation of the work to check algebraic identities and to assist in exploring and verifying proof arguments. The sentence does not say the model supplied an argument, so whether it is load-bearing is for the judging pass.
systems.basis_quote: We point out that ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Sol) was used during the preparation of this work to check algebraic identities and to assist in exploring and verifying proof arguments.

events.what_happened: Lark Song, 'Local quadratic isoperimetric stability of the truncated octahedron among parallelohedra' (arXiv:2609.03093, submitted 2 Sep 2026; 12 pp.; math.MG). Proves that the Archimedean truncated octahedron is a strict local minimiser of the isoperimetric quotient among all parallelohedra in R^3, extending the earlier lattice-Voronoi local result to the full local parameter space. Its introduction says the Cesaroni–Novaga result 'settles stability within the five-dimensional Voronoi subclass' and that the work 'does not settle Bezdek's conjecture locally'. Its later text says: 'Following the complete resolution of the truncated octahedral conjecture by Hales and Song [HS26] and independently by Cesaroni and Novaga [CN26b]...' Opened (abstract page and HTML v1 extracts).
events.delivers: Local, not global, strict minimality of the truncated octahedron among parallelohedra. Restricted to parallelohedra and to a neighbourhood. Does not address the Kelvin problem.
events.remains: Global minimality among parallelohedra (addressed by the Hales–Song and Cesaroni–Novaga preprints); everything in problem_asks.
events.doubts: Only the abstract page and extracts from the HTML were read. The paper's own citations treat the global restricted question as resolved by two preprints, which is a citation, not a verification.
events.direction: Supports local minimality of the truncated octahedron in the parallelohedral class. No direction on the Kelvin problem.

disputes.summary: Hales–Song (arXiv 1 Sep 2026) and Cesaroni–Novaga (arXiv 2 Sep 2026) prove the same restricted statement. Each says it is independent. Cesaroni–Novaga's v1 says they became aware of Hales–Song after their own work was complete. Hales–Song's text says 'Shortly after our preprint was posted to the arXiv, Cesaroni and Novaga announced an independent proof of the main result.' The two sentences are consistent with each other, and nothing in the sources contests the independence or the order. Recorded for the judging pass, not resolved.

The AI role is described differently across the sources. Hales–Song's v1 statement says the model was used 'in a substantial way at all stages of this project' and v2 says 'proof discovery'. Cesaroni–Novaga say ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Sol) was used 'to check algebraic identities and to assist in exploring and verifying proof arguments'. The tracker's paraphrase, 'substantially at every stage', is secondary and matches Hales–Song rather than Cesaroni–Novaga. Recorded as differing self-descriptions for the judging pass.

summary: Searched 36 times and opened the primary arXiv pages and HTML versions for the September 2026 results. Since 26 January 2024 no result settles the Kelvin problem or the optimality of the Weaire–Phelan structure. The in-window events are restricted. Hales and Song (arXiv:2609.00997, 1 Sep 2026) and Cesaroni and Novaga (arXiv:2609.02384, 2 Sep 2026) both prove that the regular truncated octahedron uniquely minimises surface area among three-dimensional parallelohedra of fixed volume. This is Bezdek's 2006 conjecture, which Hales and Song describe as 'a modification of the original Kelvin problem that restricts the equal-volume partitions of space to tilings by parallelohedra'. Cesaroni and Novaga write that Theorem 1.1 'does not address arbitrary periodic equal-volume partitions, and hence does not solve the Kelvin problem'. Neither paper treats Weaire–Phelan, and its two cell types with curved faces lie outside the parallelohedral class as I read it. Song's arXiv:2609.03093 (2 Sep 2026) proves local strict minimality within parallelohedra and cites both papers as a 'complete resolution' of the restricted conjecture, which is a citation and not a verification. Earlier lattice and perimeter papers (Cesaroni–Novaga 2024 and March 2026; Nobili–Novaga 2024) restate the Kelvin problem as open. Close call: whether the restricted parallelohedral result belongs to the bullet. The bullet names the Kelvin problem and Weaire–Phelan optimality, not parallelohedral tilings, and both September papers disclaim the Kelvin problem. The reading that counts it as partial progress rests on the authors calling Bezdek's problem a modification of Kelvin's. AI: Hales and Song credit 'GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT' with a substantial role in the proof, quoting their 'Statement on AI use' in v1 and describing 'proof discovery' in v2, with the authors taking responsibility for the proof and certificate. Cesaroni and Novaga credit 'ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Sol)' with checking algebraic identities and assisting in exploring and verifying proof arguments. Both preprints are unrefereed. The certificate's computer-assisted inequality has not been replayed by anyone I found, and the tracker's 'Provisional' label is a secondary aggregator and not a review. Pre-window history: Weaire and Phelan's 1993–94 counterexample to Kelvin's foam, Kusner–Sullivan's 1996 analytic comparison within Kelvin topology, Hales's 1999/2001 planar honeycomb theorem (dimension 2, analogue), Gabbrielli 2009, Itoh–Nara 2010 (restricted, orthic), Opsomer–Vandewalle 2016 (unequal volumes), Lángi 2021/2022 (mean width) and Cesaroni–Novaga 2023 (existence). Wikipedia's current article (not the January 2024 revision) says the Weaire–Phelan structure's optimality 'remains unproven'. Unverified dates and claims: 'Bollettino UMI 2026' and 'Mathematika 2025' publication status, the Hales–Song acknowledgements text (via summarising fetch), and the Pittsburgh talk's date of 10 Sep 2026 (from the seminar page). Dead end: a 2021 APS abstract (Dmitrieff) proposing a four-dimensional candidate, seen only in a search snippet, which is a different dimension. Frank–Kasper lattice comparisons (arXiv:1806.01726) were checked and not found in the abstract page; the area figures in search snippets were not verified and were not recorded as events.
competing_reading: Read the bullet as the parallelohedral (translative) equal-volume problem. The Kelvin literature itself calls Bezdek's conjecture 'a modification of the original Kelvin problem' (Hales–Song), so a judge could count the September 2026 results as settling a case of the bullet, and count the AI involvement as load-bearing. Against this: the bullet names the Kelvin problem and the optimality of the Weaire–Phelan structure. Those concern equal-volume partitions with curved faces, and Weaire–Phelan is not a parallelohedral tiling. Both September papers say they do not solve the Kelvin problem. A second reading takes the optimality clause as only 'Weaire–Phelan beats Kelvin's foam', which was settled within Kelvin topology by Kusner–Sullivan in 1996. That is a different claim from the bullet's optimality wording.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A peer-reviewed publication or independent replay of the Hales–Song exact certificate and of the Cesaroni–Novaga argument. (2) Whether the Hales–Song model's contribution is load-bearing, which needs the PDF's exact acknowledgement and statement text, not the summarised fetch. (3) A result on the full equal-volume Kelvin problem, or a proof of Weaire–Phelan's minimality among all equal-volume partitions. (4) The Kusner–Sullivan Forma paper and the Gabbrielli 2009 paper, to check their equal-volume status and areas. (5) The January 2024 revision of the Wikipedia article for the status the freeze recorded. (6) The Bollettino UMI and Mathematika publication records.
